1051.quote_or_event: “Lentils, flour and ghee - these things, I beg of You.”
1051.explanation: In his aarti hymn in Dhanasri, Bhagat Dhanna, a farmer, asks God plainly for the simple food and goods he needs. In Gurbani the one fully fitting giver to ask is God.
1051.tie_back: The Kural permits asking when one meets someone it is fitting to ask; Dhanna asks without shame because he addresses the one Giver who is always fit to be asked.
1051.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 695, Raag Dhanasri, Bhagat Dhanna (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1051._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both approve of asking the right giver, but Dhanna asks God, while the Kural means generous human beings, and the second half (blame falls on the one who refuses) has no parallel.

1052.quote_or_event: “When I am hungry, I ask for food; when I am full, I am totally at peace.”
1052.explanation: Guru Arjan speaks as a child to its parent: asking for food is natural and carries no shame, and being fed brings complete contentment.
1052.tie_back: The Kural says asking can itself be a pleasure if what is asked for comes without pain to either side; Guru Arjan pictures exactly such easy asking between a child and a loving parent.
1052.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1214, Raag Sarang, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1052._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on asking that is free of distress, but the relationship is devotee to God, not one person asking another.

1053.quote_or_event: “Balwand says that Khivi, the Guru's wife, is a noble woman, who gives soothing, leafy shade to all.”
1053.explanation: In the Ramkali ki Vaar of Satta and Balwand, Mata Khivi, wife of Guru Angad, is praised for running the Guru's langar and sheltering everyone who came. She is remembered as the model of open-hearted, dutiful giving.
1053.tie_back: The Kural says there is grace even in asking from those whose hearts hide nothing and who know their duty; Mata Khivi is the Sikh example of such a giver, whose shelter covered all who came.
1053.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar, Satta and Balwand (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1053._accuracy_note: Good portrait of the ideal open-hearted giver, but the verse praises the giver and says nothing directly about the dignity of the one who asks.

1054.quote_or_event: “The Great Giver does not hold back anything.”
1054.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak says God's gifts are beyond reckoning and the Giver keeps back not even a sesame seed's worth.
1054.tie_back: The Kural says asking is as honourable as giving when the giver would never think of withholding, even in a dream; Guru Nanak describes the Great Giver as exactly such a one, who holds nothing back.
1054.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib (Pauri 25), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1054._accuracy_note: Strong match on a giver who never withholds, but the Giver is God rather than a human patron, and the claim that asking equals giving is not made.

1055.quote_or_event: “People beg and pray, "Give to us, give to us", and the Great Giver gives His Gifts.”
1055.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak describes all creatures constantly asking and God constantly giving; asking makes sense because a Giver exists who answers it.
1055.tie_back: The Kural says people take up asking only because there are those in the world who never hold back; Guru Nanak likewise grounds all asking in the existence of the Great Giver.
1055.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib (Pauri 4), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1055._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit: asking exists because a reliable giver exists; the difference is that the giver here is God, not generous people.

1056.quote_or_event: “The Langar - the Kitchen of the Guru's Shabad has been opened, and its supplies never run short.”
1056.explanation: Satta and Balwand praise the langar of Guru Angad's court, a free kitchen open to all whose stores never run out, alongside the spiritual food of the Guru's word.
1056.tie_back: The Kural says that at the mere sight of those free from withholding, the afflictions of want vanish; the Guru's langar, whose supplies never fail, is the Sikh institution where the hungry find their want relieved.
1056.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar, Satta and Balwand (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1056._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on ungrudging, never-failing provision that ends want; the verse's primary sense is also spiritual (the kitchen of the Shabad).

1057.quote_or_event: In the Sikh langar, as Britannica describes it, everyone sits together in a straight line, neither ahead to claim higher status nor behind to mark inferiority; the institution began as a protest against caste, and under Guru Amar Das visitors ate in the casteless langar.
1057.explanation: The langar gives food freely and without any mark of contempt or rank: rich and poor, high and low caste sit side by side and are served the same meal as equals.
1057.tie_back: The Kural says the asker's heart rejoices when givers give without scorn or ridicule; the langar is built precisely so that no one who receives food is looked down upon.
1057.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sikhism: Sikh practice' (sections on the rejection of caste and the worship service) and 'Guru Amar Das'
1057._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit: the langar institutionalises giving without contempt; this is a paraphrase of Britannica's summary, not a verbatim quotation.

1058.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, the young Nanak was given money by his father to make a profitable bargain, but spent it feeding a group of hungry holy men, calling this the true bargain (sacha sauda).
1058.explanation: The story presents giving to those in need as the only trade that gives worldly dealings real worth; it is hagiography rather than documented history.
1058.tie_back: The Kural says that without askers the world's busy comings and goings would be mere puppet-motion; the Sacha Sauda story likewise implies that commerce gains meaning only when it meets the needs of those who ask.
1058.source: Janamsakhi tradition, as retold in Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, Vol. 1 (1909) (paraphrase)
1058._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the story values giving to the needy above profit, but the Kural's specific claim that askers give human activity its meaning is not made; Janamsakhi material is hagiographic, and the Macauliffe page was not re-checked in this session.

1059.quote_or_event: “He continues to give, and His Provisions never run short.”
1059.explanation: In So Dar, Guru Nanak praises God as the endless Giver whose gifts to all creatures never run out; this giving is central to how Gurbani praises God's greatness.
1059.tie_back: The Kural asks what glory givers could have if no one wished to receive; Gurbani likewise praises God above all as the Giver to countless receivers.
1059.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 9, So Dar (Rehras), Raag Asa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1059._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the verse links greatness with endless giving, but does not say, as the Kural does, that a giver's fame depends on the existence of askers.

1060.quote_or_event: “O mind, don't cry out that you are hungry, always hungry; stop complaining.”
1060.explanation: Guru Amar Das tells the mind to stop its constant cry of hunger and its complaints, and to rest in trust instead of grievance.
1060.tie_back: The Kural tells the asker not to grow angry when refused, since his own want explains his situation; Guru Amar Das likewise counsels the needy mind to give up complaint and resentment.
1060.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 27, Sri Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1060._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both forbid resentment in the one who lacks, but Guru Amar Das addresses complaint against God's provision, not anger at a human who refuses.
